questions.q: Where are RLS roles and their DAX filter expressions originally defined?
options: In Power BI Desktop, under the Modeling tab's Manage roles window
In the Fabric Admin Portal's tenant settings
In the OneLake data access role wizard
In Microsoft Purview's classification rules
questions.explain: RLS roles and their DAX filter expressions are authored in Power BI Desktop (Manage roles), then published to the service along with the model.

questions.q: Which workspace role(s) are NOT restricted by row-level security, even if listed as a member of an RLS role?
options: Admin, Member, and Contributor
Viewer only
All workspace roles are always restricted by RLS
Only Admin is exempt; Member and Contributor are still filtered
questions.explain: RLS only restricts Viewers. Admins, Members, and Contributors already have full access to the underlying data and bypass RLS filters entirely.

questions.q: What does object-level security (OLS) do that row-level security (RLS) does not?
options: Hides entire tables or columns from a role, rather than filtering rows
Filters rows dynamically based on USERPRINCIPALNAME()
Controls who can open a semantic model at all
Encrypts data at rest inside OneLake
questions.explain: OLS hides whole tables or columns from a role's visibility entirely (field list, visuals, Q&A/Copilot), while RLS only filters which rows within a visible table are shown.

questions.q: Why does this lesson show OLS configuration as a code/TOM example instead of a Fabric portal screenshot?
options: OLS has no native authoring UI in the Fabric portal or Power BI Desktop — it's set via Tabular Editor or the XMLA endpoint
Microsoft has deprecated object-level security entirely
OLS can only be configured through Microsoft Purview
Screenshots of OLS are restricted under Microsoft's licensing terms
questions.explain: Unlike RLS, OLS isn't authored anywhere in the Fabric portal or Power BI Desktop UI — it requires an external tool like Tabular Editor, or scripting the Tabular Object Model over the XMLA endpoint.

questions.q: What T-SQL statement implements row-level security directly on a Fabric Warehouse table, and how does it relate to a Power BI semantic model built on that same Warehouse?
options: CREATE SECURITY POLICY with a filter predicate — it protects direct SQL queries but doesn't automatically protect the semantic model
GRANT ROLE SECURITY — it automatically applies to any semantic model built on top
ALTER TABLE ... ENABLE ROW SECURITY — it replaces the need for RLS in the semantic model
CREATE MASKING POLICY — it masks values instead of filtering rows
questions.explain: CREATE SECURITY POLICY with ADD FILTER PREDICATE implements Warehouse-layer RLS using a predicate function. It protects anyone querying the Warehouse or SQL analytics endpoint directly, but a semantic model built on top still needs its own RLS defined separately.
